newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel tells U.S. envoy Hebron moves up to Arafat.
newsitem.headline: Israel tells U.S. envoy Hebron moves up to Arafat.

text.p: Israel told U.S President Bill Clinton's Middle East peace envoy on Sunday it was now up to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to take steps to clinch an elusive peace deal on a troop pullout in Hebron.
U.S. envoy Dennis Ross said he hoped to resuscitate talks faltering over the West Bank town and Jewish settlements. His last mediation effort collapsed in October.

Following overnight meetings with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Arafat, Ross held talks on Sunday with Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, who was quoted by his office in a statement as telling the visiting envoy:

"Israel has advanced toward compromise on some important issues on the Hebron question in the desire to bring the matter to a conclusion, and now it is up to Yasser Arafat to take similar steps." The statement did not elaborate.
The Mordechai remarks underscored comments on Friday by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher that put the onus on Arafat to finalise an accord.

Arafat, who earlier cast doubts on Ross' objectivity, said after meeting the U.S. envoy early on Sunday: "It was very constructive and fruitful and an important meeting. We discussed how to push the peace process forward in all means."
Arafat's spokesman Nabil Abu Rdainah said Ross brought several ideas aimed at closing a deal on Hebron.
Israel and the PLO accuse each other of foot-dragging in talks on the West Bank town, 80 percent of which was due to have been handed over to Arafat's Palestinian Authority months ago.

Palestinians were encouraged when Clinton last week criticised Israel's planned expansion of West Bank Jewish settlements, but Christopher's subsequent comment that Palestinians had to make gestures on Hebron irked PLO leaders.
"The most important thing is that Mr Ross has to be an accurate mediator, and not to be biased on the side of Israel," Arafat said on Friday.
Arriving late on Saturday, Ross went straight into meetings with Netanyahu in Jerusalem and with Arafat in self-ruled Gaza.

"The important thing that I am trying to do is to re-energise the peace process and then be in a position to go back in a couple of days to report back to the president," Ross told reporters on Sunday.

Negotiators for both sides met again on Sunday in a six hour session. Netanyahu wants a deal signed in 1995 changed to protect some 400 militant Jewish settlers in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs.

Abu Rdainah said Ross' ideas focused on four main points: Israel's demand to be able to pursue suspects in Palestinian areas, reopening Martyrs Street in the heart of town that was closed to Palestinians, arming Palestinian police as provided in the original accord, and joint Israeli-PLO patrols.
PLO security official Jibril Rajoub said of Israel's "hot pursuit" demand: "We will never agree to this."
The PLO wants assurances Netanyahu will carry out other deals signed by Israel's previous centre-left government once the deal on Hebron is carried out.

Violence flared again on Sunday in Hebron. Despite an army curfew imposed after a firebomb landed beside a Jewish settler home in the morning, a second petrol bomb was hurled at a nearby Israeli army position hours later.
"As a result of the blast a ladder fell and two Palestinians were injured and taken to hospital," the army said. Witnesses said troops arrested four Arab children in the area.
In the West Bank near Bethlehem, an Israeli soldiers' hitchhiking post was damaged in an explosion apparently caused by Palestinian guerrillas but no one was injured, the army said.

Clinton last sent Ross after clashes in September in the West Bank and Gaza claimed the lives of 60 Palestinians and 15 Israelis. He left after three weeks of mediation saying the sides had narrowed the gaps but failed to reach a deal.
